questions.question: A 50-year-old woman presents with excessive tearing while eating, which started a few months ago. Upon further questioning, she recalls having facial nerve palsy about a year ago, which has since improved. Based on this presentation, at what level of the facial nerve pathway did the injury most likely occur?

options.A: At the level of the geniculate ganglion
options.B: At the level of the chorda tympani
options.D: At the level of the greater petrosal nerve

explanation.text: The clinical presentation suggests Bogorad syndrome, also known as Crocodile tears syndrome, occurring due to the misdirection of parasympathetic fibres that regenerate after facial nerve injury. These fibres, which originally control salivation, are misdirected to the lacrimal gland, leading to involuntary tear production during eating.

The injury that leads to this phenomenon typically occurs around the geniculate ganglion, where the parasympathetic fibers for both salivation and lacrimation are present. Damage here can lead to a mix of motor and sensory dysfunction, including taste disturbances and autonomic dysfunction.

A- Suprageniculate lesions B- Suprastapedial lesions C- Infrastapedial lesions D- Infrachordal lesions Course of Facial Nerve Segment Description Clinical Significance (Topodiagnostic tests help in determining the location of facial nerve lesion) Intracranial (Cisternal) Emerges from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, medial to CN VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve). Lesions can cause facial weakness or paralysis.

Intratemporal Meatal Segment It enters the internal acoustic meatus with CN VII I and the nervus intermedius. Vulnerable to compression in acoustic neuromas. Labyrinthine Segment (Most common site for facial nerve palsy.) Extends from the internal acoustic meatus to the geniculate ganglion; limited blood supply. Damage can affect taste and hearing. Tympanic Segment Runs horizontally through the middle ear cavity above the oval window and stapes.

Injury in this segment may lead to altered middle ear function and hearing. Mastoid Segment Longest segment; descends vertically through the mastoid bone, giving off branches like the nerve to stapedius and chorda tympani (anterior 2/3 tongue) Injury can lead to facial nerve dysfunction, including Bell's palsy. Extratemporal Stylomastoid Foramen It exits the skull and enters the parotid gland.

Damage here leads to facial muscle weakness but spares glands and taste. Parotid gland Divides into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical branches to innervate facial muscles. The nerve passes through but does not innervate the parotid. Facial nerve injury during parotid surgery causes facial paralysis.

Topodiagnostic tests Key points Schirmer test Decreased lacrimation indicates a lesion proximal to the geniculate ganglion. Stapedial reflex It is lost in lesions above the nerve to stapedius. Taste test Impairment of taste indicates a lesion above the chorda tympani. Submandibular salivary flow test Decreased salivation shows injury above the chorda tympani.

questions.question: A 35-year-old male presents with difficulty chewing and pain near his temporomandibular joint (TMJ) after sustaining blunt trauma to the side of his face. Upon examination, there is tenderness over the ramus of the mandible. Which muscle is most likely affected?

explanation.text: Masseter covers the ramus of the mandible, making it most likely to be affected by trauma to the side of the face, as described in the scenario. Its primary action is elevating the mandible, which is essential for biting and chewing. Anatomy of the mandible: The largest and strongest bone in the face. Parts of the Mandible: Body: Horizontal portion of the mandible. Alveolar process: Holds the lower teeth.

Mental protuberance (chin) and mental foramen (allows passage of nerves and vessels). Mylohyoid line: For muscle attachment. Rami: Vertical portions on each side. Coronoid process: Attachment for the temporalis muscle. Condylar process: Forms the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) by articulating with the temporal bone. Mandibular Canal: Runs inside the mandible from the mandibular foramen to the mental foramen.
Houses the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels supplying the lower teeth.

Muscles of mandible Muscle Location Action Nerve Supply Masseter Covers the ramus of the mandible Elevates the mandible for biting and chewing Mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3) Temporalis Attached to the coronoid process Elevates and retracts the mandible Lateral Pterygoid Located in the infratemporal fossa Protracts and depresses the mandible and moves it laterally.
Medial Pterygoid It runs parallel to the masseter on the inner side of the ramus of mandible. Elevates and assists in protrusion of the mandible

questions.question: A 34-year-old male presents with difficulty opening his mouth following a jaw injury. Which of the following muscles is primarily responsible for opening the mouth?

explanation.text: The scenario describes trauma to the muscles responsible for depressing the jaw and opening the mouth, particularly the lateral pterygoid muscle. Muscles of mastication They are responsible for moving the mandible at the temporomandibular joints during the process of chewing. They are divided into: Principal muscles Accessory muscles Temporalis Masseter Lateral pterygoid Medial pterygoid Digastric Buccinator Mylohyoid Geniohyoid.

Characteristic features: Situated in or around the infratemporal fossa and originate from the mesoderm of the first pharyngeal arch. They attach to the ramus of the mandible and are innervated by the mandibular nerve, a branch of the trigeminal nerve.

**Principal muscles of mastication Origin Insertion Nerve supply Action Masseter (Option A):** Superficial layer (largest): Zygomatic arch (anterior 2/3rds of the lower border) and adjoining zygomatic process. Middle layer: Zygomatic arch (lower border of posterior 1/3rd). Deep layer: Zygomatic arch (deep) surface. Superficial layer: Ramus of the mandible (lower part of lateral surface). Middle layer: Ramus of mandible (central part). Deep layer: Ramus of the mandible (rest of the part) Masseteric nerve (Anterior division of mandibular nerve) Elevates the mandible (close the mouth).

**Protrusion Temporalis (Option B):** Temporal fossa (excluding zygomatic bone) Temporal fascia Coronoid process Ramus of mandible (anterior border). Deep temporal nerves (Anterior division of mandibular nerve) Elevates mandible (close the mouth) Side-to-side (grinding) movement Retraction of mandible Lateral pterygoid (Option D) Upper head (smaller): Infratemporal surface and crest of greater wing (sphenoid bone) Lower head (larger): lateral pterygoid plate (lateral surface) Pterygoid fovea (neck of mandible) Articular disc (anterior margin) and capsule of temporomandibular joint A branch from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve Depresses mandible (open the mouth) Protrusion Turns chin to the opposite side (right lateral pterygoid turns chin to left) Medial pterygoid (Option C) Superficial head: tuberosity of maxilla and adjoining bone Deep head: lateral pterygoid plate (medial surface) and adjoining surface of palatine bone Angle (rough area on the medial surface) and adjoining ramus of the mandible. Nerve to medial pterygoid (main trunk of the mandibular nerve) Elevates the mandible (close the mouth) Protrusion Grinding movement

questions.question: A 48-year-old female with diabetes presents with severe, sharp right-sided facial pain triggered by light touch, along with numbness and tingling. Examination shows hyperesthesia and decreased sensation on the right side. Which of the following structures is most likely involved in this condition?

explanation.text: The given scenario suggests a lesion of the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. The trigeminal nerve is associated with four nuclei (1 motor and three sensory).

Nuclear columns of Trigeminal nerve (Extends throughout the brainstem) General somatic afferent column: Has three nuclei Spinal nucleus of Vth nerve (Option A) Principal sensory nucleus of Vth nerve (Option D) Mesencephalic nucleus (Option C) Fibers conveying pain and temperature sensations from the majority of the facial area synapse at this location.

Fibers transmitting touch and pressure sensations synapse in this nucleus This nucleus extends into the midbrain and receives proprioceptive impulses from the muscles of mastication, the temporomandibular joint, and the teeth.

Special visceral efferent column: Motor nucleus of the Vth nerve (Option B) These fibres supply the muscles derived from the first pharyngeal arch, namely the muscles of mastication, the mylohyoid, the anterior belly of the digastric, the tensor palatini and the tensor tympani.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman presents with sudden numbness, tingling, heaviness, dull pain, and heightened sensitivity on the right side of her face. Examination shows reduced sensation in the right maxillary and mandibular areas, with intact motor function and no other deficits. From which location does the affected cranial nerve emerge?

explanation.text: The presented scenario suggests a lesion at the sensory root of the trigeminal nerve, which originates from the pons. Trigeminal nerve (Cranial nerve V) The largest and thickest mixed nerve, containing both sensory and motor components.

It is associated with four nuclei (1 motor and 3 sensory) and three primary divisions as: Ophthalmic division Maxillary division Mandibular division Course: Midbrain (Option A) is the origin of cranial nerves III (oculomotor nerve) and IV (trochlear).
**Cerebrum (Option B):** is the origin of cranial nerves I (Olfactory nerve) and II (optic nerve).
**Medulla oblongata (Option D):** is the origin of cranial nerves IX (glossopharyngeal nerve), X (vagus nerve), XI (accessory nerve), and XII (hypoglossal nerve).

questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with a progressively enlarging mass in his neck. He has a history of heavy smoking and reports recent difficulty swallowing. A biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma of the base of the tongue. Which of the following lymph nodes is most likely to be involved in the initial spread of cancer from this region?

explanation.text: The base of the tongue drains primarily into the jugulodigastric node, which is part of the deep cervical lymphatic chain. Deep Lymphatics of the Head and Neck Deep Cervical Nodes: Final drainage points for lymph from the head and neck. Located along the carotid sheath. Divided into superior and inferior groups. Deep Lymphatic Drainage Pathways: Lymphatics generally follow major vascular structures.

Superficial cervical nodes: Along external jugular vein. Deep cervical nodes: Along internal jugular vein. Specific pathways: Tongue: Drains into jugulodigastric and jugulo-omohyoid nodes (near lingual artery). (Option A) Thyroid gland: Drains into pretracheal, paratracheal, and deep cervical nodes (along inferior thyroid artery). (Options C & D) Infratemporal fossa: Drains into superior deep cervical nodes (near maxillary artery branches).

Clinical Significance: Infection spread: Lymphatic networks allow infections to travel through spaces like the retropharyngeal and parapharyngeal spaces, reaching the mediastinum. Cancer staging: Involvement of deep cervical nodes helps stage head and neck cancers, crucial for treatment decisions. Cancers from the lungs and upper GI tract may spread to supraclavicular nodes.
**Supraclavicular node (Option B):** Typically involved in cancers of the lungs and upper GI tract.

questions.question: A 65-year-old patient presents with a neck mass and difficulty swallowing. On imaging, the mass is located in the area bordered by the internal jugular vein, scalenus anterior muscle, and longus colli muscle. Which lymph node group is most likely located in this area?

explanation.text: Chassaignac's Triangle, defined by the internal jugular vein, scalenus anterior muscle, and longus colli muscle, contains the Level IV (Lower Jugular) nodes, which are important in the diagnosis of head and neck cancers. Cervical Lymph Nodes: Location, Drainage, and Clinical Significance Lymph Node Structure: Arranged in two horizontal rings and two vertical chains on each side of the neck.

Outer, superficial ring: Includes occipital, preauricular (parotid), submandibular, and submental nodes. Inner, deep ring (Waldeyer's ring): Composed of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) in the nasopharynx and oropharynx. Vertical chain: Along the carotid sheath, divided into superior and inferior groups. Drainage Pathways: All lymph from head and neck drains into deep cervical nodes, either directly or via other nodes.
Superficial cervical nodes along the external jugular vein drain into deep cervical nodes.

Classification of Deep Cervical Nodes (Crucial for Cancer Spread): Level Location Significance I (Option A) Submental, submandibular triangles Divided into IA (submental) and IB (submandibular) II (Option B) Upper jugular (skull base to hyoid bone) Drains upper portion of internal jugular vein and accessory nerve III (Option C) Middle jugular (hyoid to omohyoid/cricothyroid) Surrounds middle third of internal jugular vein IV Lower jugular (from omohyoid/cricothyroid to clavicle) Drains lower third of internal jugular vein V Posterior triangle Divided into Va (upper) and Vb (lower), near accessory nerve Specific Drainage Points: Tongue lymph drains into submental, submandibular, jugulodigastric, and jugulo-omohyoid nodes.

Jugulodigastric node: Key in tongue drainage, often enlarged in tonsillitis. Chassaignac's Triangle: Formed by internal jugular vein, scalenus anterior, and longus colli muscles. Contains Level IV and scalene nodes, important in cancer diagnosis. (Option D) Clinical Importance of Lymphatic Drainage Patterns: Guides surgical and radiation approaches in head and neck cancer.

Lung cancers may spread to both supraclavicular nodes, while upper GI cancers spread to left supraclavicular nodes. Venous Circulation Connection: Lymph returns to systemic circulation via the right and left lymphovenous portals at the internal jugular and subclavian junctions. Right jugular trunk: Drains lymph from right arm, thorax, head, and neck into the right lymphatic duct or jugulo-subclavian junction.
Left jugular trunk: Drains into the thoracic duct or directly into internal jugular or subclavian vein.

questions.question: During surgery, the surgeon notices an additional thyroid vein, known as the Kocher’s vein, which drains into the internal jugular vein. The surgeon carefully ligates this additional vein to avoid any postoperative complications. What is the most likely origin of this additional vein?

options.A: Between the middle and inferior thyroid veins
options.B: Between the superior and inferior thyroid veins

explanation.text: The Kocher’s vein originates between the middle and inferior thyroid veins.

Venous drainage of the Thyroid Gland: Vein Origin Drainage Superior Thyroid Vein The upper pole of the thyroid Internal jugular vein Middle Thyroid Vein Middle of the thyroid lobe Internal jugular vein Inferior Thyroid Vein The lower border of the isthmus Plexus in front of trachea → Left brachiocephalic vein Kocher's Vein (Fourth Thyroid Vein) Between middle and inferior veins (Option A) Internal jugular vein

questions.question: During a thyroidectomy, the surgeon identifies an artery supplying the lower part of the thyroid isthmus, originating from the arch of the aorta. What is the name of this artery?

explanation.text: Rarely (in about 3% of cases), the thyroid gland receives additional blood supply from the thyroidea ima artery, which can originate from the brachiocephalic trunk or the arch of the aorta and enters the lower part of the isthmus.
**Accessory thyroid arteries (Option A):** arising from tracheal and esophageal arteries also supply the thyroid.
**The Middle thyroid artery (Option B):** does not exist.
**The inferior thyroid artery (Option C):** does not arise from the arch of aorta.

questions.question: A patient presents with the following symptoms: when sticking out the tongue, it deviates towards the left side, and there is noticeable atrophy on the left side of the tongue. Based on the image, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Injury to the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) leads to tongue weakness or paralysis on the affected side. The tongue will deviate toward the side of the injury when protruded. In this case, the leftward deviation of the tongue and atrophy on the left side of the tongue suggest a left-sided hypoglossal nerve injury. Hypoglossal Nerve Lesions: Types of Lesions: Nuclear Lesion: Damage at the hypoglossal nucleus.

Supranuclear Lesion: Damage above the hypoglossal nucleus (e.g., cerebral cortex, corticobulbar tract, internal capsule, cerebral peduncles, pons). Infranuclear Lesion: Damage to the motor axons of the nerve. Symptoms of Lesions: Paralysis: Weakness of tongue muscles. Fasciculations: Scalloped tongue appearance. Atrophy: Muscle wasting of the tongue over time.

Effects of Lesion Location: Unilateral Lesions: Tongue deviates towards the damaged side when protruded (due to stronger genioglossus muscles on the opposite side). Partial compensation by the intact hypoglossal nerve. Supranuclear Lesions: Tongue deviates away from the affected side when protruded (due to upper motor neuron crossing). No atrophy, but causes slow, spastic tongue movements. Often caused by strokes or pseudobulbar palsy.

Infranuclear and Nuclear Lesions: Cause ipsilateral tongue atrophy and weakness. May cause fasciculations. Impact of Lesions: Unilateral Lesions: Usually not serious; remaining nerve compensates. Bilateral Lesions: Can severely affect speech and swallowing due to inability to protrude the tongue. Causes of Hypoglossal Nerve Damage: Unilateral Damage: Tumors, infections, trauma (e.g., surgical trauma from carotid endarterectomy).
Bilateral Damage: Rare, often from radiation therapy.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the nerve supply of the four types of papillae on the tongue is incorrect?

options.A: Filiform papillae are primarily innervated by the lingual nerve (branch of the mandibular nerve) for general sensation.
options.B: Fungiform papillae are innervated by the chorda tympani (branch of the facial nerve) for taste sensation.
options.C: Circumvallate papillae are innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve for both taste and general sensation.
options.D: Foliate papillae are innervated by the vagus nerve for taste sensation.

explanation.text: The foliate papillae are actually innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (for taste sensation), not the vagus nerve. The vagus nerve is involved in other sensory functions, but it does not innervate the taste buds of the foliate papillae. Sensory Nerves: The lingual nerve is the nerve of general sensation and the chorda tympani is the nerve of taste for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue except vallate papillae.

The glossopharyngeal nerve is the nerve for both general sensation and taste for the posterior one-third of the tongue including the circumvallate papillae. The posteriormost part of the tongue is supplied by the vagus nerve through the internal laryngeal branch Papillae Types and Nerve Supply: Filiform Papillae (FL): Function: Most numerous, provide texture. Appearance: Whitish, keratinized. Nerve Supply: Lingual nerve (general sensation).

Fungiform Papillae (FG): Function: Contain taste buds. Appearance: Red, vascularized. Nerve Supply: Chorda tympani (facial nerve, CN VII) for taste; Lingual nerve for sensation. Circumvallate Papillae (CV): Function: Largest, contain taste buds. Structure: Surrounded by cleft, contain Von Ebner glands. Nerve Supply: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) for taste and sensation. Foliate Papillae: Function: Contain taste buds.
Appearance: Vertical folds, prominent in animals. Nerve Supply: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) for taste; Lingual nerve for sensation.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes are primarily involved in the drainage of lymphatic vessels from the dorsal region of the tongue?

explanation.text: Dorsal lymphatic vessels of the tongue typically drain into the jugulodigastric nodes. Lymphatic Drainage of the Tongue Region Drainage Pathways Nodes Involved Marginal Submental Route: Descends beneath mucosa, drains into submental nodes. Jugulodigastric and Jugulo-omohyoid Route: Vessels pierce mylohyoid, follow hypoglossal nerve vein to jugulodigastric and jugulo-omohyoid nodes.

Submandibular Route: Crosses sublingual gland, pierces mylohyoid, drains into submandibular nodes; may also target jugulodigastric or jugulo-omohyoid nodes. Posterior Marginal: Traverses pharyngeal wall to jugulodigastric nodes.

**Submental (Option A):** Jugulodigastric Jugulo-omohyoid Submandibular (Option B) Central Ascending Route: Vessels ascend between genioglossus fibers, accompany lingual veins to deep cervical nodes. Submandibular Route: Some vessels pierce mylohyoid and drain into submandibular nodes. Deep cervical nodes (Jugulodigastric, Jugulo-omohyoid) Dorsal Posteroinferior Course: Vessels run posteroinferiorly, with bilateral drainage near the midline. Convergence with Marginal: Joins marginal vessels, pierces pharyngeal wall. Direct Jugulo-omohyoid Drainage: Descends behind hyoid, penetrates thyrohyoid membrane, terminates in jugulo-omohyoid node.

**Jugulodigastric (Option C):** Jugulo-omohyoid Clinical Implications Bilateral Drainage: Comprehensive neck management needed for lingual malignancies. Predicting Tumor Spread: Understanding patterns aids in accurate staging and therapy planning.
**Subclavicular nodes (Option D):** These nodes are not directly involved in the drainage from the tongue. They are more related to the drainage from the upper limb and part of the thorax.

questions.question: Which lymphoid tissue is not a part of Waldeyer’s ring?

explanation.text: Submandibular lymph nodes are part of the superficial lymphatic ring, not Waldeyer’s ring. Waldeyer's Ring: Definition: Inner, deep ring of lymphatic tissue in the head and neck Composed of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) Location: Situated in the nasopharynx and oropharynx Guards the entrance to respiratory and digestive tracts Components: (Options A, B & D) Major Components: Palatine tonsils,

Nasopharyngeal tonsil (adenoid), Lingual tonsil Less Prominent Components: Tubal tonsils, Lateral pharyngeal bands Functions: Traps pathogens inhaled or ingested Initiates immune responses by activating lymphocytes and generating antibodies Generation of B cells: Germinal centers in the tonsils play a critical role in B cell production Clinical Significance: Susceptible to infections, e.g., tonsillitis involving palatine tonsils Potential site for tumors such as lymphoma

questions.question: A surgeon is performing a neck dissection and encounters the internal jugular vein. Which of the following structures does not directly drain into the internal jugular vein?

explanation.text: The maxillary vein drains into the retromandibular vein, which ultimately contributes to the external jugular vein, not the internal jugular vein.

Head and Neck Venous Drainage: Vein Type Primary Drainage Area Main Tributaries Destination Superficial veins Scalp, face, and occipital scalp Posterior retromandibular vein Posterior auricular vein Submandibular veins External, anterior, or posterior external jugular veins External jugular vein Scalp and face Posterior retromandibular vein Posterior auricular vein Subclavian vein Anterior jugular vein Submandibular region Superficial submandibular veins External jugular or subclavian vein Posterior ext. jugular Occipital scalp - External jugular vein Deep veins Skull, brain, face, and neck Inferior petrosal sinus, facial, lingual, and pharyngeal veins Superior & middle thyroid veins Internal jugular or subclavian vein Internal jugular vein Skull, brain, face, and neck Inferior petrosal sinus, facial, lingual, pharyngeal, and thyroid veins (Options A, B & D) Subclavian vein Subclavian vein Arm and neck External jugular, dorsal scapular, and anterior jugular (sometimes) Brachiocephalic vein Retromandibular vein Face Maxillary vein, superficial temporal vein (Option C) External jugular or facial vein

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant is evaluated after a complicated delivery in which upward traction was applied to the arm. The parents report that the infant’s left hand has fingers curled and cannot extend them. On examination, the left eyelid droops, and the pupil is smaller. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The Infant displays signs of Klumpke's Palsy, such as claw hand deformity and Horner syndrome, which suggests that the C8-T1 nerve roots are involved. Lower Trunk (inferior): C8 & T1 roots join to form a lower trunk.

Klumpke's Palsy Injury: C8, T1 Features: Claw Hand Deformity Affected Muscles: Lumbricals & interossei Action: MCP Flexion IP Extension Injury Result: MCP Extension IP Flexion Horner Syndrome:(T1) Ptosis: Drooping of the eyelid due to paralysis of the superior tarsal muscle (Muller muscle) Miosis: Constricted pupil due to paralysis of the dilator pupillae Nerve Involvement: Lower trunk injury (C8, T1) Median nerve: Partial injury Ulnar nerve: Total compromise T1 sympathetic fibres affected Mechanism of Injury: Hyper-abduction of the arm Falls (e.g., holding a branch) Birth injuries Erb's Palsy (Option A): It involves the upper trunk (C5-C6), leading to the classic "waiter's tip" posture, not the symptoms described.
**Radial Nerve Palsy (Option C):** Would cause wrist drop, not the claw hand or Horner syndrome.
**Ulnar Nerve Injury (Option D):** This does not typically result in Horner syndrome.

questions.question: A 65-year-old male presents with complaints of dizziness, syncope, and numbness in his left arm during physical activity. On examination, his left radial pulse is weak, and the blood pressure in the left arm is significantly lower than in the right arm. What is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism behind this patient's symptoms?

options.A: Retrograde blood flow in the left vertebral artery due to subclavian artery stenosis
options.B: Reduced blood flow in the left subclavian artery due to thoracic aortic dissection
options.C: Retrograde blood flow in the left internal carotid artery due to basilar artery stenosis
options.D: Retrograde blood flow in the right vertebral artery due to subclavian artery stenosis

explanation.text: The clinical scenario described above is suggestive of subclavian steal syndrome. Obstruction to the subclavian artery proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery may lead to retrograde blood flow in the left vertebral artery.

Subclavian steal Syndrome: Pathophysiology: Causes Atherosclerosis (most common) Takayasu disease (least common) Giant cell arteritis Blalock Taussig shunt Thoracic aortic dissection Thoracic outlet compression Interrupted aortic arch Congenital aortic coarctation Risk Factors Smoking, diabetes, obesity, lack of exercise, unhealthy diet, family history More common in individuals who are biologically male Complications Upper limb ischemia, neurological problems Asymptomatic Numbness of arm extends to fingertips (most frequent) Vertebrobasilar artery insufficiency Presyncope/syncope, neurologic deficits Upper extremity claudication Tingling sensation/numbness in the face Decreased blood pressure on the affected side Transient hemiparesis (weakness) of the affected side Diagnosis BP in left arm < BP in right arm Pulse in left arm < pulse in right arm CT angiography (Investigation of Choice) Doppler ultrasound scan Treatment Balloon stenting, angioplasty Endarterectomy

questions.question: Which of the following arteries does not supply the upper part of the tonsil?

explanation.text: The upper part of the tonsil is supplied by the ascending pharyngeal, descending palatine, and the greater and lesser palatine arteries. Ascending palatine artery does not contribute to the blood supply of the upper part of the tonsil, instead, it predominantly supplies the lower part.

Blood Supply of the Tonsil: Artery Branch of Region Supplied Tonsillar artery Facial artery (sometimes Ascending Palatine artery) Palatine tonsil and posterior lingual musculature Dorsal lingual branches Lingual artery Anterior tonsillar region Ascending palatine artery (Option B) Facial artery Posterior tonsillar region (lower part) Ascending pharyngeal artery (Option A) External carotid artery Upper part of the tonsil (posterior) Descending palatine artery (Option C) Maxillary artery Upper part of the tonsil Greater and Lesser Palatine arteries (Option D) Descending palatine artery Upper part of the tonsil

questions.question: A 12 y/o boy presents with nasal bleeding, after nose-picking. On examination, the bleeding site is located in the anterior nasal septum, and the diagnosis of epistaxis from Kiesselbach's plexus is made. Which of the following arteries is LEAST likely to contribute to the bleeding from this plexus?

explanation.text: Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area) is the most common site of epistaxis due to its rich vascular supply.

Arteries that contribute to this plexus include: Anterior ethmoid artery Septal branches of the superior labial artery and greater palatine artery Sphenopalatine artery Arteries contributing to Kiesselbach’s plexus: Artery Branch of Region Supplied Anterior ethmoid artery (Option A) Ophthalmic artery Anterosuperior portion of the nasal septum Sphenopalatine artery (Option D) Maxillary artery Posteroinferior portion of the nasal septum Septal branch of superior labial artery (Option C) Facial artery Caudal septum and columella Greater palatine artery Maxillary artery Anteroinferior portion of the nasal septum Blood Supply of the Nasal septum: The posterior ethmoid artery (Option B) supplies the posterosuperior nasal septum and does not contribute to the vascular supply of Kiesselbach’s plexus.

questions.question: Which statement about the maxillary artery is false?

options.A: It arises behind the neck of the mandible.
options.B: The middle meningeal artery passes through the foramen ovale.
options.C: The posterior superior alveolar artery supplies upper molar teeth.
options.D: The sphenopalatine artery is the artery of epistaxis.

explanation.text: The middle meningeal artery transmits through the foramen spinosum, not the foramen ovale. Contents of the Foramen Ovale: (Mnemonic: MALE) Mandibular nerve (V3): The third division of the trigeminal nerve, responsible for motor and sensory functions to the lower face. Accessory meningeal artery: A small artery that supplies the meninges.

Lesser petrosal nerve: A branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) that carries parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland. Emissary veins: These veins connect the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid venous plexus. Maxillary Artery Definition: A larger terminal branch of the external carotid artery, arises behind the neck of the mandible (Option A). Distribution: Supplies a wide territory.

It has 3 parts First Part Deep Auricular Anterior Tympanic Middle Meningeal Transmits: Foramen spinosum Clinical significance: A ruptured middle meningeal artery (MMA) is the most common cause of an epidural hematoma (EDH).

Accessory Meningeal Inferior Alveolar Transmits: Mandibular foramen Distribution: Lower 8 teeth and mylohyoid muscle Second Part Masseteric Distribution: Masseter muscle Deep Temporal Distribution: Temporalis muscle Pterygoid Distribution: Lateral and medial pterygoids Buccal Distribution: Skin of the cheek Third Part Posterior Superior Alveolar (Option C) Distribution: Upper molar and premolar teeth and gums Infraorbital Greater Palatine Distribution: Soft palate, tonsil, palatine glands, mucosa of upper gums Pharyngeal Artery of Pterygoid Canal Sphenopalatine Distribution: Lateral and medial walls of nose, various sinuses.
Clinical Significance: Known as the artery of epistaxis (Option D).

questions.question: Identify the marked branch of the External carotid artery?

explanation.text: Lingual artery: A major branch of the external carotid artery. Supplies the tongue and the oral floor. Arises anteromedially from the external carotid artery. Located at the tip of the greater horn of the hyoid bone, between the superior thyroid artery and the facial artery.

External Carotid Artery Origin: Terminal branch of the common carotid artery Position: Anterior to the internal carotid artery Function: Chief artery supplying the front of the neck and face Branches: Anterior Branches (3) Superior Thyroid Artery: Supplies the thyroid gland. Lingual Artery: Supplies the tongue. Facial Artery: Supplies the face. Posterior Branches (2) Post Auricular Artery: Supplies the auricle (outer ear).

Occipital Artery: Supplies the occiput (back of the head). Terminal Branches (2) Maxillary Artery: Supplies the maxilla (upper jaw) and deep facial structures. Superficial Temporal Artery: Supplies the temporal region and scalp. Medial Branch (1) Ascending Pharyngeal Artery: Supplies the pharynx and tonsils.
